Section 3 • Transmitted Flux

3.2 Mapping the Observed Wavelengths to the Local Gas Frame

The central question of this subsection is the following: given a photon that is eventually detected by an observer with wavelength \(\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}\), what wavelength is locally associated with that same photon when it crosses a gas element at comoving position \(\vec{x}\)? This mapping is essential because the gas does not respond directly to the wavelength measured by the observer, but to the wavelength locally seen in its own frame. Once this local wavelength is known, one can determine how close the photon is to a resonance transition and therefore how efficiently it can be absorbed.

To make this relation explicit, let us consider an observer frame, denoted by “obs”, located at \(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{obs}}\), with associated scale factor \(a_{\mathrm{obs}} = a(\vec{x}_{\mathrm{obs}})\). We denote by \(\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}\) the wavelength with which a given photon is measured by the observer’s spectrograph. Before reaching the observer, however, that photon has propagated through the universe along a null geodesic, and its wavelength has evolved with position due to cosmological expansion and additional relativistic effects. Our goal in this subsection is therefore to express the wavelength locally associated with the photon at each point \(\vec{x}\) along its trajectory in terms of the observed wavelength \(\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}\).

3.2.1 Cosmological Redshift

We begin by accounting only for the effect of cosmic expansion. Consider a photon that is eventually detected by the observer with wavelength \(\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}\). At an earlier point \(\vec{x}\) along its trajectory, the wavelength locally associated with that same photon is \begin{align} \lambda'\left(\vec{x}\right) = \lambda_\mathrm{obs}\,\frac{a\left(\vec{x}\right)}{a_\mathrm{obs}}. \tag{3.4} \end{align} This simply makes explicit the fact that the wavelengths of detected photons at “obs” are redshifted with respect to their wavelength in the past: the further the \(\vec{x}\) position along their trajectory we look at, the more blueshifted these photons would be.

3.2.2 Doppler Effect

The previous expression accounts only for the background expansion. If the gas element at \(\vec{x}\) also has a peculiar line-of-sight velocity \(v_{i\,\parallel}(\vec{x})\), then the wavelength relevant for the interaction with that gas must include an additional Doppler shift. The corresponding local wavelength is 1: \begin{align} \lambda'\left(\vec{x}\right) = \lambda_\mathrm{obs}\,\frac{a\left(\vec{x}\right)}{a_\mathrm{obs}} \Dop^{-1}(\vec{x}), \qquad \Dop(\vec{x}) \coloneqq \sqrt{\frac{1-\beta\left(\vec{x}\right)}{1+\beta\left(\vec{x}\right)}}, \qquad \beta\left(\vec{x}\right) \coloneqq \frac{v_{i\,\parallel}\left(\vec{x}\right)}{\cc}. \tag{3.5} \end{align} Therefore, the local wavelength is obtained by combining the cosmological scaling with the Doppler correction induced by the peculiar motion of the gas. This expression could be further modified by including additional relativistic corrections, such as gravitational potential effects. However, in this work, we will consider any further contributions negligible.

3.2.3 Velocity Units

The quantity introduced in this subsection is not a new physical velocity of the gas. Rather, it is a convenient reparametrization of the observed spectral coordinate (for more details check appendix B). Its main advantage is that, when the spectrum is expressed in logarithmic wavelength units, redshift acts as an additive shift (rather than multiplicative), and the separation between different transition lines becomes independent of the redshift at which the absorption occurs (see B.1).

Although the observer naturally measures photons in wavelength or frequency units, it is often useful to introduce the following logarithmic coordinate, commonly referred to as velocity units: \begin{align} v_\dagger \;=\; c\ln\!\left( \frac{\lambda'(\vec{x})}{\lambda_\dagger} \frac{a_\dagger}{a(\vec{x})} \right) = c\ln\!\left( \frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}}{\lambda_\dagger} \frac{a_\dagger}{a_{\mathrm{obs}}} \right), \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \lambda_{\mathrm{obs}} = \lambda_\dagger\, \frac{a_{\mathrm{obs}}}{a_\dagger}\, \exp\!\left(\frac{v_\dagger}{c}\right), \tag{3.6} \end{align} where \(\lambda_\dagger\) is a chosen anchor wavelength and \(a_\dagger\) is a reference scale factor. Therefore, \(v_\dagger\) should be understood simply as a relabelling of the observed spectral axis.

Substituting this change of variable into Eq. 3.5, the wavelength locally associated with the photon at position \(\vec{x}\) becomes \begin{align} \lambda'\left(\vec{x}\right) = \lambda_\dagger\, \exp\!\left(\frac{v_\dagger}{c}\right)\, \frac{a\left(\vec{x}\right)}{a_\dagger}\, \Dop^{-1}\left(\vec{x}\right). \tag{3.7} \end{align}

As previously mentioned, the usefulness of velocity units comes from the fact that, employing this logarithmic coordinate change, the separation between two different emission/absorption lines becomes redshift independent (proof on B.1).

Additionally, by introducing a separate anchor wavelength normalization for different lines, \((i,j)\), corresponding to their rest-frame absorption, and setting the anchor redshift \(a_\dagger = a_f\), it is possible to re-express the different absorption processes in a common relative line-centered velocity range (see B.2): \begin{align} \lambda'_j\left(\vec{x}\right) = \lambda_j\, \exp\!\left(\frac{v_\dagger}{c}\right)\, \frac{a\left(\vec{x}\right)}{a_f}\, \Dop^{-1}\left(\vec{x}\right). \tag{3.8} \end{align} In this coordinate system all lines span the same velocity interval: for a skewer travelling from \(a(x_\mathrm{em}) = a_\mathrm{em}\) to \(a(x_{f}) = a_f\), the absorptions (neglecting peculiar velocities) would appear in the range: \begin{align} v_\dagger \in \left[ 0, \; c\ln\left(\frac{a_f}{a_{\mathrm{em}}}\right) \right]. \tag{3.9} \end{align}

3.2.4 Approximated Velocity Units

There is another closely related choice of spectral coordinate often employed in practical Ly\(\alpha\)-forest calculations, and it is essentially the one implemented in packages such as fake_spectra. In this case one does not keep the exact logarithmic mapping between the observed wavelength and the local gas frame across the full light cone. Instead, one fixes a single simulation snapshot at redshift \(z_{\mathrm{box}}\), assumes that the factor \(H(z)/(1+z)\) varies only mildly across the box, and tabulates the spectrum directly on a uniform velocity grid. If \(L_{\mathrm{box}}\) denotes the comoving box size along the line of sight and \(N_{\mathrm{bins}}\) the number of spectral pixels, one may write \begin{align} u_n = n\,\Delta u, \qquad \Delta u = \frac{u_{\max}}{N_{\mathrm{bins}}}, \qquad u_{\max}\approx L_{\mathrm{box}}\, \frac{H(z_{\mathrm{box}})}{1+z_{\mathrm{box}}}. \tag{3.10} \end{align} Thus, the observed spectrum is labelled directly by a velocity-like coordinate \(u\), rather than by \(\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}\) itself.

Within this approximation, a gas element located at line-of-sight position \(x_{\parallel}\) is first assigned a Hubble-flow coordinate \begin{align} u_H(x_{\parallel}) \approx \frac{H(z_{\mathrm{box}})}{1+z_{\mathrm{box}}}\, (x_{\parallel}-x_\dagger), \tag{3.11} \end{align} and is then shifted to a redshift-space position by its peculiar velocity: \begin{align} u_{\mathrm{abs}}(x_{\parallel}) = u_H(x_{\parallel}) + s_v\,v_{i\,\parallel}(x_{\parallel}), \qquad s_v=\pm 1. \tag{3.12} \end{align} Here \(s_v\) is a sign-convention parameter: its value depends only on the adopted orientation of the spectral axis and on the sign convention used for the line-of-sight peculiar velocity. In the specific convention used by fake_spectra, the absorber-centered coordinate is implemented with a plus sign.

The important point is that the calculation is then carried out directly in velocity units. For a spectral pixel labelled by \(u\), the relevant detuning from resonance is \begin{align} \Delta u(x_{\parallel};u) = u-u_{\mathrm{abs}}(x_{\parallel}), \tag{3.13} \end{align} so that the local line profile is evaluated as a function of \(\Delta u\), or equivalently of the dimensionless ratio \(\Delta u/b_i\), where \(b_i\) is the local Doppler width parameter of the absorbing gas. To first order, this is equivalent to the frequency-space description, since \begin{align} \nu_j(x_{\parallel},u) \approx -\frac{\Delta u(x_{\parallel};u)}{\lambda_j}. \tag{3.14} \end{align} Therefore, the practical single-snapshot implementation may be understood as the velocity-space version of the same construction introduced above: the spectral axis is discretized directly in velocity units, the gas element is moved to redshift space by its peculiar velocity, and the line profile is evaluated from the difference between the pixel coordinate \(u\) and the absorber-centered coordinate \(u_{\mathrm{abs}}\).

It is also useful to emphasize that, in this practical formulation, the same velocity grid is used for all transitions. The dependence on the specific line \(j\) enters through the rest-frame wavelength, oscillator strength, damping coefficient, and thermal/microturbulent broadening parameters, but not through a separate choice of spectral axis for each transition. A more explicit derivation of these relations, and of their connection with the exact wavelength mapping introduced above, is presented in Appendix C.

From this point onward, we denote by \(\Lambda\) the spectral coordinate used by the observer. Depending on the context, \(\Lambda\) may represent either the observed wavelength \(\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}\), the exact logarithmic velocity coordinate \(v_\dagger\), or one of its local approximations introduced for practical calculations. Accordingly, \(\lambda'(\vec{x},\Lambda)\) denotes the wavelength locally associated with the photon labelled by \(\Lambda\) when that photon passes through the point \(\vec{x}\). This notation allows the subsequent expressions to be written independently of the particular spectral parametrization adopted.
